(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States

No. 25-6623
HAMED KIAN, PETITIONER
v.
STATE OF FLORIDA

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL
OF FLORIDA, FOURTH DISTRICT

BRIEF FOR THE UNITED STATES
AS AMICUS CURIAE SUPPORTING RESPONDENT

INTEREST OF THE UNITED STATES
This case presents the question whether the Court
should overturn its decision in Williams  v. Florida, 399
U.S. 78 (1970), and hold that the Sixth Amendment right
to trial “by an impartial jury,” U.S. Const. Amend. VI,
requires a jury of exactly 12 people.  Although federal
criminal juries generally consist of 12 people, federal
courts may permit a jury of 11 to return a verdict if there
is good cause to excuse a juror after deliberations have
begun.  Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(1) and (3).  The United
States accordingly has an i nterest in the resolution of
this case.
INTRODUCTION
 As this Court has repeatedly recognized, the Sixth
Amendment right to  “trial, by an impartial jury” does
not constitutionalize every feature of the jury trial as it

2

existed in the Founding Era.  Instead, the Amendment
constitutionalizes only those practices that were so definitional to the very concept of a “jury” as to be incorporated in to the Amendment’s textual guarantee.  And as
this Court correctly held more than 50 years ago in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970) , the historical practice of trying criminal cases before exactly 12 jurors —
not 11 or 13 —is not one of those features .
 Although Founding Era crimes were tried before 12 -
person jur ies, the public meaning of the Amendment’s
text does not require a body of 12 .  And the common-law
preference for 12 jurors was merely a historical accident, of uncertain origin,  that did not advance the role
of the jury .  In that respect, it is much more like the
historical features of the jury that were not preserved
in the Sixth Amendment —like the requirement that jurors be all men —than it is like the historical features of
the jury that were constitutionalized —like the requirement that criminal juries be unanimous.
 Since the mid -19th century, States have allowed for
juries of fewer than 12 members in trials of serious
crimes.  And the Court’s 7 -1 decision affirming such authority  is a backbone of trial practice.  A majority of
States now use smaller juries to try at least some offenses to which the Sixth Amendment right attaches.
Overturning Williams  would call into question hundreds, if not thousands , of posttrial convictions pending
on direct review across the country.  Petitioner offers
no sound basis to reverse course on the law and cause
such disruption.
 At a minimum, this Court should not call into question a court’s ability to accept a verdict from fewer than
12 jurors in emergency circumstances .  Federal Rule of
Criminal Procedure 23(b)(3) permits a court to take a

3

verdict from 11 jurors if one is dismissed for good cause
during deliberations.   That remedy is a solution to problems that arise during  long, complex trials and deliberations, which would have been anomalous at  the time of
the Founding .  The Sixth Amendment would therefore
not speak to that remedy, and contains nothing that
prohibits it .
STATEMENT
1. The Sixth Amendment to the Federal Constitution provides that “[i]n all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right to a speedy and public trial,
by an impartial jury of the state and district wherein the
crime shall have been committed.”  U.S. Const. Amend .
VI.  The Jury Trial Clause applies to the States through
the Fourteenth Amendment.  Duncan v. Louisiana , 391
U.S. 145, 156 (1968).  And t his Court has held that the
jury-trial guarantee extends to all defendants accused
of “serious crimes .”  Id. at 161.  An offense qualifies as
“ ‘serious, ’ ” and thus triggers the Sixth Amendment
jury right, “where imprisonment for more than six
months is authorized.”  Baldwin v. New York , 399 U.S.
66, 6 9 (1970) (plurality opinion ); see Blanton v. City of
North Las Vegas , 489 U.S. 538, 542 (1989).
In Williams  v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970), this Court
considered “whether the constitutional guarantee of a
trial by ‘jury’ necessarily requires trial by exactly 12
persons, rather than some lesser number” —six, in Florida’s case.   Id. at 86.  The Court observed that at that
time, five States “provide[d] for juries of less than 12 in
felony cases” and nearly ten more States “provide[d] for
less than 12 -man juries in trials of certain offenses carrying maximum penalties of one year’s imp risonment.”
Id. at 98 n.45.  And  after examining historical understandings and other considerations, the Court held  that

4

“the 12-man panel is not a necessary ingredient of ‘trial
by jury’  ” within the meaning of the Sixth Amendment.
Id. at 86; see id. at 103.
Today, seven States provide for juries with fewer
than 12 members in felony cases, and at least  20 additional States provide for juries of fewer than 12 for misdemeanors that qualify as “serious” offenses triggering
the Sixth Amendment jury -trial right.  See p p. 16-17,
infra.  Florida remains one of the former States, providing by statute that while “[t]welve persons shall constitute a jury to try all capital cases ,” “six persons shall
constitute a jury to try all other criminal cases.”  Fla.
Stat. § 913.10.
In federal court, a criminal jury generally “consists
of 12 persons” unless the parties stipulate otherwise.
Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(1) and (2).  Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 23(b)(3) provides, however, that “[a]fter
the jury has retired to deliberat e, the court may permit
a jury of 11 persons to return a verdict, even without a
stipulation by the parties, if the court finds good cause
to excuse a juror.”
2. Petitioner was a licensed chiropractic doctor who
practiced chiropractic medicine in Jupiter, Florida.
Trial Tr. 177, 240.   Under Florida law, the state Department of Health is authorized to issue an emergency order suspending a practitioner’s license if it “finds that
immediate serious danger to the public health, safety,
or welfare requires emergency suspension.”  Fla. Stat .
§ 120.60(6).  On October 28, 2021, petitioner was personally served with such an emergency order.  See Trial Tr.
127-130; Confidential ROA 119-131 (detailing basis for
emergency suspension).

5

In December 2021, while his license was suspended,
petitioner practiced chiropractic medicine on three different patients on a total of five separate occasions.  See
Trial Tr. 165, 181, 188, 193, 200 -201.  Petitioner’s unauthorized practice of chiropractic medicine came to the
attention of state authorities after one of petitioner’s female patients filed a police report stating that petitioner
had kissed her on the lips without her c onsent during
one of the unlawful sessions .  See id. at 122, 208.  The
State of Florida subsequently filed an information
charging petitioner with five counts of practicing chiropractic medicine with a suspended license, in violation
of Fla. Stat. § 460.411(1)(b).   See Trial Tr. 14 -15.  That
offense is a third -degree felony under Florida law , Fla.
Stat. § 460.411(1), with a maximum penalty of  five years
of imprisonment.  Id. § 775.082(3)(e).
Pursuant to Fla. Stat. § 913.10, the case proceeded
to trial before a six -person jury.  During the two -day
trial, the State called several witnesses, including the
three patients treated in December 2021.  Trial Tr. 179,
192, 198.  Petitioner also testifie d in his own defense.
Id. at 238.  After hearing all the evidence, the jury found
petitioner guilty o f all five counts.  Id. at 313-314; see
Judgment 1.  The trial court sentenced petitioner to 366
days of imprisonment (with credit for 292 days served),
to be followed by ten years of probation.  Sent. as to
Counts 1, 2, and 5 ; Sent. as to C ount 3, at 3; Sent. as to
Count 4, at 3.
Petitioner appealed his conv iction on two theories :
that insufficient evidence  was presented at trial, and
that Florida’s use of a six -person jury violates the Sixth
Amendment.  Pet. Dist. Ct. Br. 10 -22.  Petitioner
acknowledged that he did not raise the jury -size issue

6

before the trial court, but he argued that facial challenges to Florida statutes could not be forfeited on appeal.  See id. at 16 -17.  The Florida Fourth District
Court of Appeal summarily affirmed in a per curiam order.  Pet. App. 2.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
More than half of the States hold trials for at least
some serious crimes before juries with fewer than 12
members.  As this Court recognized more than half a
century ago in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970),
that widespread practice is constitutional .  P etitioner
provides no sound basis for the extensive disruption
that overruling Williams would cause.  And he does not
even attempt to challenge the independent constitutionality of Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 23(b)(3),
which permits a verdict from an 11-person jury when one
juror is dismissed for good cause during deliberations.
I. As this Court has long recognized, t he Sixth
Amendment  did not constitutionalize all “the particular
forms and procedure” of jury practice “used at common
law” during the Founding Era.   United States  v. Wood,
299 U.S. 123, 143 (1936).   The 12-member jur y, whose
historical origins are uncertain , was not among the
practices enshrined in the Amendment’s text .
The word “jury” itself did not mean a 12 -member
body, and was used during the Founding Era to describe factfinding bodies of different sizes.  Also, unlike
the requirement of a unanimous verdict , the historical
practice of using 12 jurors —not 11 or 13—was never understood to advance the purposes of the jury.  And, for
over 175 years, States have been experimenting  with
jury size , confirming that 12 jurors is not an essential
ingredient of a trial by jury .

7

Every traditional stare decisis factor strongly favors
retaining  Williams .  The Court  in that case extensively
analyzed  constitutional text, history, and prior precedent.  It reached the correct result and , at a minimum,
cannot be characterized as “egregiously wrong.”   Williams also accords with  longstanding  precedent holding
that the Constitution did not freeze in place every
Founding Era jury practice.  And the Court has continued
to rely on Williams  in later cases, including to hold that
12-person juries  are not required  in federal civil trials.
 The reliance interests in retaining Williams  are
substantial .  At least 27  States use smaller juries to try
at least some serious offenses to which the Sixth
Amendment jury -trial right attaches.  Overruling Williams would thus require a majority of States to reexamine their laws  and would call into question  the validity of all cases in those States that are currently pending on direct review after such a jury trial .  Williams  is
not causing any real -world harm that justifies such upheaval.
Petitioner ’s counterarguments lack merit.  He argues that this Court need not even analyze the stare decisis factors because the logic of Williams  was eroded
by Ramos v. Louisiana , 590 U.S. 83, 89 (2020) , which
abrogated Apodaca  v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972), to
hold that criminal juries must be unanimous .  But Ramos’s critiques of Apodaca  do not apply to Williams ,
and unanimity and jury size do not rise and fall together.  Moreover , petitioner’s historical evidence establishes , at most, that criminal juries historically  had
12 people —not that the 12-person jury was so embedded in the very concept of a “jury” as to be incorporated

8

in the Sixth Amendment.  And petitioner fails to confront, let alone refute,  the strength of the reliance interests at issue here .
II.  At all events, the emergency procedures authorized by Rule 23(b)(3)  would be constitutional even independent of Williams .  Although the common -law remedy for juror dismissal was  typically  retrial before a
jury of 12, remedies like the completion of deliberations
by the remaining 11 members of a jury have evolved as
trials have become longer and more complex.   And they
are of a piece with other deliberation -related practices
on which the Sixth Amendment is silent.
ARGUMENT
As the Court held more than five decades ago in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970),  a size of precisely
12 members is one of many “incidental ” (indeed, “accidental”) common-law features  that is not enshrined in
the Sixth Amendment’s Jury Trial Clause.  Id. at 91; see
id. at 103.  Petitioner provides no  sound justification for
overturn ing that longstanding precedent —along with
the jury procedures of a majority of the  States—by
holding now that the 12 -member feature has , in fact ,
“been immutably codified into our Constitution,”  id. at
90.  Much less does he provide a reason why Federal
Rule of Criminal Procedure 23(b) (3), which permits a
jury that begins deliberations with 12 members to finish
with 11 if a juror is excused for good cause, would be
invalid.  See Pet. Br. 13 n.4.   This Court should affirm,
or, at a minimum, issue a decision that does not call Rule
23(b)(3) into question.

9

I. THIS COURT SHOULD REAFFIRM THAT THE SIXTH
AMENDMENT DOES NOT REQUIRE A JURY OF  EX-
ACTLY 12
The Sixth Amendment provides, in relevant part,
that defendants accused of serious crimes shall enjoy
“the right to a speedy and public trial, by an impartial
jury of the State and district wherein the crime shall
have been committed.”  U.S. Const. Amend. VI.  In Williams, this Court held that “the constitutional guarantee of a trial by ‘jury’  ” does not require “trial by exactly
12 persons.”  399 U.S. at 86.  That understanding —
which is supported by constitutional text, history, and
state practice —is correct.  Williams  has also engendered extensive  reliance interest s in the States.  Especially in light of those reliance interests, petitioner cannot justify  overturn ing Williams .
A. This Court Has Correctly Recognized That The  Guarantee Of “Trial By An Impartial Jury” Does Not Immutably Fix The Number Of Jurors At  Exactly  12
The Sixth Amendment does not constitutionalize
every feature of the jury trial from common law or the
Founding —otherwise, myriad aspects of modern jury
practice would be unconstitutional.  Instead, the Amendment incorporates only those features of the historical
jury trial that are embedded in the very meaning of a
“trial, by an impartial jury,” U.S. Const. Amend. VI.  The
practice of having juries with 12 members, which lacks
any practical historical justification , is one of the many
historical features that does not meet that standard .

10

1. The Sixth Amendment  does not constitutionalize
every feature of  Founding Era common -law jurytrial practice
The Sixth Amendment guarantees a right to “trial,
by an impartial jury” in the district where the crime occurred, but it “says nothing else about what a ‘trial by
an impartial jury’ entails.”  Ramos v. Louisiana , 590
U.S. 83, 89 (2020).  In constructing the right, t his Court
has looked first to  “the historical role of the jury at common law .”  Oregon v. Ice, 555 U.S. 160, 170 (2009) .  In
doing so, it has found that certain aspects of common -
law practice are so inherent to its role that they are implicitly incorporated into the concept of trial by “jury.”
Among those are  “the right to have the jury, rather than
the judge, reach the requisite finding of ‘guilty,’  ”  Sullivan v. Louisiana , 508 U.S. 275, 277 (1993); see United
States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506, 51 0 (1995); and, under
this Court’s recent decision in Ramos, the “right to a
unanimous verdict,” 590 U.S.  at 100.  At the same time,
the Court has made clear that the Sixth Amendment did
not constitutionalize all “the particular forms and procedure used at common law .”  United States  v. Wood,
299 U.S. 123, 143 (1936).
Just because “a given feature existed in a jury at
common law in 1789,” that does not mean that “it was
necessarily preserved in the Constitution.”  Williams ,
399 U.S. at 92-93.  Instead, the Framers themselves understood and expected that a reference to trial by jury
would not constitutionalize every contemporaneous
jury practice.  For example, “the common -law ‘vicinage’
right  * * *  presumptively entitled defendants to a jury
of the ‘neighbourhood’ where the crime was allegedly
committed.”  Smith v. United States , 599 U.S. 236, 246
(2023) (quoting 4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on

11

the Laws of England  344 (1769)).  But although that
right was “highly prized by the founding generation,”
id. at 248, it was not inherent in the guarantee of “Trial
* * * by Jury” in Article III’s Venue Clause, U.S. Const.
Art. III, § 2, Cl. 3.  See Smith, 599 U.S. at 248.  Nor, by
the same logic,  would it be inherent in the Sixth Amendment right to “trial , by an impartial jury ,” U.S. Const .
Amend. VI.  Instead, the Framers explicitly added a vicinage requirement through a separate clause.  See
Smith, 599 U.S. at 248.
Consistent with the understood limitations on the
Constitution’s use of the word “jury,” this Court has
identified many other features of the common -law jury
trial that are not inherently incorporated into the Constitution’s guarantee of trial “by jury” or “by an impartial jury.”  At common law, juries exclusively consisted
of property -owning men.  See John H. Langbein, The
English Criminal Trial Jury on the Eve of the French
Revolution, in The Trial Jury in England, France, Germany 1700-1900, at 24-25 (Antonio Padoa Schioppa ed. ,
1987).  Those rules also prevailed in the States during
the Founding Era.  See Albert W. Alschuler & Andrew
G. Deiss, A Brief History of the Criminal Jury in the
United States , 61 U. Chi. L. Rev. 867 (1994).  But this
Court has long recognized that “[t]he Sixth Amendment
does not preclude legislation making women qualified to
serve as jurors in criminal prosecutions , although that
was not permitted at common law.”  Wood, 299 U.S. at
145.  Indeed, the Court ultimately interpreted the Sixth
Amendment to require that women be eligible for  the
jury pool.  Taylor v. Louisiana , 419 U.S. 522, 536 (1975).
Similarly, although common -law juries were “kept
together without meat , drink, fire , or candle, till they

12

are agreed,” 2 Matthew Hale, Historia Placitorum Coronae 297 (1736), “[c]ourts are no longer required to impose these requirements on juries,” Dietz v. Bouldin,
579 U.S. 40, 52 (2016).   In addition, while Founding Era
juries decided questions of both fact and law, see  Matthew P. Harrington, The Law-Finding Function of the
American Jury, 1999 Wis. L. Rev. 377, 423 -425, this
Court has long restricted  criminal juries from deciding
pure legal questions , see Sparf v. United States , 156
U.S. 51, 102 (1895).   Nor are all jury-selection pr ocedures enshrined:  although peremptory challenges were
an important feature of Founding Era jury trials,
4 Blackstone 346 , the Court has held that the Constitution does not “require[  ] the Congress to grant peremptory challenges to defendants in criminal cases ,” Stilson
v. United States , 250 U.S. 583, 586 (1919).  And there
are additional examples as well .  See Wood, 299 U.S. at
143 (collecting other examples).
2. The Sixth Amendment does not require a jury of exactly 12 jurors
As this Court recognized in Williams, although
common-law criminal juries “consisted of 12,” 399 U.S.
at 91, that historical feature is one of the many that was
not ossified in the Sixth Amendment , see id. at 103.
Constitution al text, structure, and history;  the origins
and nature of the 12-person requirement ; and historical
state practic e all make that clear.
a. The original  public meaning of the word “jury”
was not limited to 12-person bodies.  Although criminal
cases were tried by 12 -person juries at common law , the
word “jury” itself more broadly referred to  a group
“sworn to enquire into any matter and declare the truth
according to evidence.”  John Ash, The New and Complete Dictionary of the English Language  535 (1775) ;

13

see Giles Jacob , A New Law Dictionary  (9th ed. 1772)
(Jacob Dictionary ) (explaining that “Jury   * * *  [s]ignifies a certain ”—unspecified —“number of men  sworn to
inquire of, and try the matter of fact, and declare the
truth upon such evidence as shall be delivered them” )
(emphasis omitted).
Accordingly, Founding Era readers would have had
no trouble understanding a group of a different size as
constituting a “jury.”   For example, in a lecture extolling “the trial by jury,” James Wilson said, “ [w]hen I
speak of juries, I feel no peculiar predilection for the
number twelve ,” observing that the “grand jury consists of more, and its  number is not precisely fixed. ”
2 James Wilson, Collected Works of James Wilson  954
(Kermit L. Hall & Mark David Hall eds. , 2007).  Blackstone similarly described a type of inquest as “done by
a jury of no determinate number; being either twelve,
or less, or more.”  3 Blackstone  258 (1768).
Notwithstanding that indeterminacy , t he Sixth
Amendment  simply refers to a “jury ,” without specifying its size.  That drafting choice contrasts with the
specificity of other provisions , like the “twenty dollar[  ]”
threshold for the civil jury -trial right , U.S. Const.
Amend. VII; the designation of “two Senators from each
State,” Art. I, § 3; and the careful rules for determining
the number of Representatives ,  Art. I, § 2 .  It also contrasts with the Sixth Amendment’s own specific ity on
other aspects of the jury:  both its “impartial[ity] ” and
its genesis  in “the State and district wherein the crime
shall have been committed .”  Amend. VI.  And t he
Amendment’s silence as to jury size  is especially  telling
because the Framers, when founding their new nation,
were on notice of  trial juries of other sizes.

14

For example, a lthough 12-person juries were typically used in English and American  criminal trials, it
was the “Custom” “in Wales” to “try by six Jurors.”  1
Giles Duncomb, Trials per Pais  96 (1766).  And under
British rule  in the Colonies  before the Revolution,
smaller juries had also been imposed  occasionally , at
least in civil cases .  See H. Richmond Fisher, The Seventh Amendment and the Common Law: No Magic in
Numbers , 56 F.R.D. 507, 529 (197 3); Resp. Br. 13 -15.  If
the Framers or the First Congress wanted to prevent
such practices from taking root in American criminal
trials, they could have expressly specified a jury of 12—
as, for example, some colonial charters  and the Virginia
Declaration of Rights had done .  See , e.g., Va. Decl. of
Rights § 8 (1776), reprinted in 7 The Federal and State
Constitutions 3813 (Francis Newton Thorpe ed., 1909)
(Thorpe).  Instead, the Sixth Amendment notably omitted any mention  of a 12-juror requirement .
b. Nothing in the history or nature of common -law
practice compels the conclusion that a “jury” must inherently be sized at exactly at 12.  The origins of 12 -person
juries are unclear, with commentators frequently  justifying the practice simply on the ground that “the number of twelve is much respected in holy writ, as 12 apostles, 12 stones, 12 tribes, etc.”  1 Edward Coke, First
Part of the Institutes  of the Laws of England , § 234, at
*155a (1812  ed.); see Duncomb 92; see also Pet. Br. 5 -6.
Whatever the true origins , the specific number 12 has
no obvious purpose, see Williams , 399 U.S. at 88 , which
distinguish es it from other features of historical jury
practice that this Court has deemed to be embedded in
the guarantee of  a “trial by jury .”
Jury u nanimity , for example,  was understood  at the
Founding  to further  the jury trial’s purpose of checking

15

prosecutorial power , by ensuring that the guilty verdict
represents “the judgment of the whole society” rather
than only a subset sympathetic to the government.  2 Wilson 961; see Duncan v. Louisiana , 391 U.S. 145, 156
(1968); Williams , 399 U.S. at 100 n.46 .  The unanimity
requirement  thus “relate[s] to” the “substance ,” Wood,
299 U.S. at 143 , of the jury -trial right .  By contrast, the
historical preference for  exactly 12 jurors—not 11 or
13—was merely a matter “of form ,” ibid., the justification for which is at best unclear.   That type of happenstance formality is unlikely to be genuinely definitional
to the very nature of a “trial by an impartial jury .”  See
ibid.
c. State practice beginning in the 19th century confirms the nonuniversality of understanding a right to
trial by “jury” as a guarantee of a 12 -member body.
Whether by constitution or by statute, a majority of
States have through the years allowed trials by juries
smaller than 12 for various serious offenses to which the
Sixth Amendment’s  jury-trial right attaches —i.e., felonies and/or misdemeanors for which “imprisonment for
more than six months is authorized,” Baldwin v. New
York, 399 U.S. 66, 69 (1970)  (plurality opinion) ; see Callan v. Wilson, 127 U.S. 540, 549 (1888)  (noting that the
class includes some misdemeanors) .
Michigan ’s 1850 constitution , for example, provide d
that “[i]n every criminal prosecution the accused shall
have the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury, which may consist of less than twelve men in
all courts not of record”  if so authorized by the legislature.  Mich. Const. Art. I V, § 46; Art. VI, § 28 (1850),
reprinted in 4 Thorpe 1949, 1956.  The referenced courts
had jurisdiction over some serious misdemeanor offenses, see Mich.  Comp. Laws §§ 118.3924, 181.5762

16

(1857), and Michigan’s specification of juries smaller
than 12 existed alongside its textual requirement of
“trial by an impartial jury.”   A subsequent constitutional
amendment by Louisiana, while worded so as to treat a
12-member “jury” as the default, adopted a similar
practice of allowing the legislature to authorize  trial “by
a jury” of “less than twelve ,” for certain serious crimes.
La. Const. Art. 7 (1879) , reprinted in  3 Thorpe 1472.
Accordingly, t he second half of the 19th century saw
several States expressly prescribe juries of fewer than
12 for a number of  serious offenses .  For example, pursuant to the constitutional provision discussed above, an
1880 Louisiana statute  provided for  smaller juries for
certain serious offenses.  See State v. Demouchet , 3 So.
565 (La. 18 88) (discussing Act 35 of 1880).  Florida and
Utah both provided for smaller juries for noncapital felonies.  See 1877 Fla. Laws, ch. 3010, § 6; Utah Const. Art.
I, § 10 (1895), reprinted in 6 Thorpe 3703.   And Texas
provided for juries of fewer than 12 in the courts with
jurisdiction over misdemeanor offenses.  See Tex. Const.
Art. V, § 17 (1876), reprinted in 6 Thorpe 3640.  Texas’s
provision, like Michigan ’s, was not worded in a manner
that treated the word “jury” as inherent ly a body of 12 .
See Tex. Const. Art. V, § 17 (1876) (“A jury in the county
court shall consist of six men. ”); see also Resp. Br. 19-
20 (citing additional 19th -century provisions) .
Today, a majority  of the States authorize trial for  at
least some serious crimes in front of juries of fewer than
12.  Seven States use smaller juries for at least some
felonies.  See Ariz. Rev. Stat.  Ann. § 21-102(B); Conn.
Gen. Stat.  Ann. § 54-82(c); Fla. Stat. §  913.10; Ind. Code
Ann. § 35 -37-1-1(b); La. Const. Art. I, §  17(A); Mass.
Gen. Laws  Ann. ch. 218, §  26A; Utah Code  Ann. § 78B-
1-104(1)(b)  and (c).  At least 20  additional States use

17

smaller juries to try misdemeanors —including misdemeanors that are serious rather than petty offenses .
See, e.g., Alaska Stat. Ann. § 22.15.150; N.Y. Crim. Proc.
Law §  360.10(A); Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 33.01; Va.
Code Ann. § 19.2-262(B); Wash. Rev. Code Ann.
§ 2.36.010(13). *  And Congress has authorized criminal
trials in tribal courts by juries of “ not less than six persons.”  15 U.S.C. 1302(a)(10).
That tradition of  experimentation  distinguishes the
historical size of 12  from other features of the jury trial
that are constitutionalized in the Sixth Amendment.
For example, only a handful of States have ever permitted nonunanimous juries  in serious criminal cases —a
strong indicator  that unanimity is embedded in the very
concept of a  “trial by jury .”  See Burch v. Louisiana ,
441 U.S. 130, 138 & n.12 (1979); Ramos, 590 U.S. at 88.
By contrast, S tates have recognized  for more than  175
years that they can provide their citizens with a trial by
“jury” without requiring a jury of exactly 12.   That understanding accords with the core original meaning of
the Sixth Amendment’s text .
B. No Sound Reason Exists To Overturn  William s
More than half a century ago, this Court in Williams
upheld the very same Florida six -person jury rule that
petitioner now challenges .  See 399 U.S. at 80 n.3.  Petitioner, however, would have the Court cast aside that
longstanding precedent, and the more than 175 years of

Idaho Crim. R. 23(c) ; Kan. Stat. Ann. § 22-3404(2); Ky. Rev. Stat.
Ann. § 29A.280(1); Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.8355; Minn. Gen. R. Prac.
802(f ); Miss. Code Ann. § 11-9-143; Mont. Code Ann. § 46-17-201(1);
Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-2705(2); N.M. Stat. Ann. § 35-8-3(A); Okla. Stat.
Ann., tit. 22 , § 601; Or. Rev. Stat.  Ann. § 136.210(2); W. Va. Code
§ 50-5-8(d); Wyo. R. Crim. P. 23 .

18

state practice that it has sustained, in favor of a rigid
definition of “jury” as invariantly comprising exactly 12
people.  That request is unsound.  Although “ stare decisis is ‘not an inexorable command,’  ” Janus v. AFSCME
Council 31 , 585 U.S. 878, 917  (2018) (citation omitted) ,
“even in constitutional cases, a departure from precedent ‘demands special justification,’  ” Gamble v. United
States, 587 U.S. 678, 691 (2019)  (citation omitted) .
There is no such justification here .  Indeed, factors that
the Court has looked to in deciding whether to overrule
other precedent —the nature of any error , consistency
with related decisions and subsequent legal developments, reliance interests, and the decision’s workability
and real-world consequences , s ee Dobbs v. Jackson
Women’s Health Organization , 597 U.S. 215, 268
(2022), all counsel against overruling  Williams .
1. Nothing in Williams ’s reasoning justifies overruling
it
The Court in Williams devoted extensive attention
to the “history of the development of trial by jury in
criminal cases,” 399 U.S. at 86 -87; to “[t]his Court’s earlier decisions,” id. at 90; and to “the relevant constitutional history,” id. at 92.  In reviewing the common -law
history, the Court acknowled ged that “sometime in the
14th century the size of the jury at common law came to
be fixed generally at 12 .”  Id. at 89. But it found “that
particular feature of the jury system appears to have
been a historical accident, unrelated to the great purposes which gave rise to the jury in the first place.” Id.
at 89-90.  And it ultimately rejected the proposition that
“this accidental feature  of the jury  has been immutably
codified into our Constitution ,” id. at 90; see id. at 103.
Although petitioner criticizes the reasoning of Williams, see Br. 29-34, he fails to refute its central pillars.

19

First, it is indisputable that not “every feature of the
jury as it existed at common law —whether incidental or
essential to that institution —was necessarily included
in the Constitution wherever that document referred to
a ‘jury.’ ”  Williams , 399 U.S. at 91.  As discusse d above,
see pp. 11-12, supra, interpreting “jury” to refer solely
to juries as they were at common law would mean that
every jury would consist of property -owning men
locked away without heat or sustenance.  Not even petitioner takes that extreme position.  Second, petitioner
cannot explain why the exact size of 12 —not a person
more or a person less —is an “essential” feature, rather
than an “incidental”  or “accidental” one, Williams , 399
U.S. at 90-91. See Pet. Br. 5 -11.  He offers no meaningful basis for its existence  and no evident reason, other
than historical practice itself , why the Framers would
have considered 12  superior to 11, 13, or other reasonable products of legislative judgment.
For the better part of two centuries, States have
deemed it possible  to have a trial by a “jury” that does
not consist of  exactly 12 jurors.  See pp. 15-16, supra.
At a bare minimum , it was  not “grievously or egregiously wrong ,” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 121 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring in part) , for this Court in Williams to take
the same view .  And “[a] garden -variety error or disagreement does not suffice to overrule.”  Id. at 121 -122
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part) .
2. Williams  is consistent with  related decisions  and
subsequent legal developments
Williams is also not the sort of  outlier decision that
can easily be discard ed without unduly disrupting other
precedent.  Well before Williams , a long line of precedent recognized  that the Constitution did not freeze in
place every aspect of the Founding Era jury .  See, e.g.,

20

Wood, 299 U.S. at 143; Patton v. United States , 281 U.S.
276, 30 6 (1930) (rejecting common -law jury -trial rule
that “ was justified by conditions which no longer exist”); Glasser v. United States , 315 U.S. 60, 85 (1942).
The Court had long taken the same approach to the Seventh Amendment  civil jury -trial right .  See Galloway  v.
United States , 319 U.S. 372, 390 -392 (1943) .  Williams
simply applied that same approach to the size of the
jury.  See 399 U.S. 90 -103.
 In doing so, the Court did not just “ignore[  ],” Knick
v. Township of Scott , 588 U.S. 180, 203 (2019) , prior decisions that could be seen to have addressed the same
issue, as outlier decisions sometimes do.   The Court instead explained  that while “earlier decisions” had
“assumed” —“often in dictum” —that 12-member juries
were “immutably codifie d into our Constitution,”  those
decisions  rested on the flawed supposition  “that every
feature of the jury as it existed at common law” was
“necessarily included in the Constitution .”  Williams ,
399 U.S.  at 90-92.  “Noticeabl y absent” from those  earlier decisions was an actual analysis of whether an immutable size of 12 is an “essential” feature inherent in a
trial by “  ‘jury,’  ” id. at 91—an analysis that Williams
then conducted , see id. at 91-103.  Williams ’s reasonable first-in-time application of that analytical framework does not make it an outlier.
 Indeed, t his Court has never retreated from Williams’s holding —instead, it has reiterated and built
upon it .  For example, while “at least five Members of
the Court” in Ballew v. Georgia, 435 U.S. 223 (1978) , believed that a jury smaller than six is not permissible fo r
serious crimes , Burch, 441 U.S. at 133, 137 , the lead
opinion by Justice Blackmun expressly stated that  “we
adhere to, and reaffirm our holding in Williams ,”

21

Ballew, 435 U.S. at 239 .  The Court also affirmatively
relied on Williams  to conclude that the Seventh
Amendment right to “trial by jury” in civil cases also
does not require a 12-person jury .  Colgrove  v. Battin,
413 U.S. 149, 157 (1973).  And the Court likewise  relied
on Williams  to uphold Massachusetts’s “two -tier system” of jury trials, under which a criminal defendant
was first tried before a judge and then, if found guilty,
tried before a jury.  See Ludwig v. Massachusetts , 427
U.S. 618, 620 -621, 625 (1976) ; see also Gaudin, 515 U.S.
at 510 n.2  (citing Williams ); Batson v. Kentucky , 476
U.S. 79, 85 n.6 (1986)  (same).
3. Overruling  Williams  would disrupt significant  reliance interests
Williams ’s position in the jurisprudential framework makes this a case in which “reliance provides a
strong reason for adhering to established law ,” Janus,
585 U.S. at 926.  Overruling Williams  could “throw into
doubt” other “previous decisions from this Court ,” Hilton v. South Carolina Pub. Rys. Comm’n , 502 U.S. 197,
203 (1991) , like the holding that civil juries need not
have 12 members. That holding informs the current
Federal Rules, which provide that  federal civil jury trials must “begin with at least 6 and no more than 12
members,” Fed. R. Civ. P. 48(a), and the predominant
practice of in fact having  civil juries smaller than 12.
See Steven S. Gensler et al., Better by the Dozen:
Bringing Back the Twelve -Person Civil Jury , 104 Judicature 47, 49 -50 (2020).
But even if limited solely to the size of juries in trials
of serious criminal offenses,  an about -face on Williams
would have a highly disruptive effect.   As discussed
above, at least 27 States currently use juries of fewer
than 12 for serious crimes:  seven States use such juries

22

for felonies, and at least another 20 use them for at least
some misdemeanors to which the Sixth Amendment
jury-trial right attaches.  See p p. 16 -17 & n. *, supra.
Overruling Williams  would thus “require an extensive
legislative response” in the States , Hilton, 502 U.S. at
203, which “possess substantial reliance interests in
their existing  [criminal -procedure] schemes,” Erlinger
v. United States , 602 U.S. 821, 870 (2024) (Kavanaugh,
J., dissenting).
That, however, would be the least of the States’  problems.  The more overwhelming one is that o verturning
Williams  would also cast doubt on  hundreds if not thousands of nonfinal  convictions  in cases tried before
smaller juries .  Although  a new procedural rule would
not disturb final convictions, it would “apply to cases
pending in trial courts and on direct review .”  Edwards
v. Vannoy, 593 U.S. 255, 27 6 (2021).  Under Florida law,
only capital cases require 12 -person juries.  See Fla.
Stat. § 913.10 .  Accordingly,  Florida explains that many
of its thousands of  cases currently pending on direct review are from six-person jury trials.  Resp. Br. 32; cf. Fla.
Office of the State Cts . Admin., Florida’s Trial Courts:
Statistical Reference Guide  FY 2024 -25 3-20 ( Dec.
2025), https://perma.cc/9HV2 -WM9A (1413 convictions
following  jury trial in Florida circuit courts , which handle felonies,  during a single year ).  Across the other
States that use smaller juries, there may be hundreds ,
if not thousands , more cases pending on direct appeal
that were tried before juries  smaller than 12 .
The number of convictions at stake is much larger
than in Ramos, which only affected the practices in two
States (Louisiana and Oregon), and only in the subset
of their nonfinal convictions where the jury was not
unanimous.  See 590 U.S. at 108.   Reversing course here

23

is therefore likely to  cause “wildly more[  ] disruption ,”
id. at 109 , than the Court predicted there.  Depending
on state forfeiture and prejudice rules, convictions from
trials with smaller juries may be subject to retrial before a 12-person jury even if the defendant did not press
the issue below.  Cf. Henderson  v. United States , 568
U.S. 266, 268 (2013) (holding that error is “plain” for
purposes of federal law so long as it is “plain” by “the
time of appellate review”).   Retrying even a significant
subset of those cases  could burden both  state prosecutors and the state courts with a massive amount of duplicative work.  And as witnesses’ memories fade  and
evidence dissipates , there is a real risk that some , perhaps many,  cases would not be able to be retried, leading to an unjustified windfall for offenders convicted of
serious crimes .
4. Williams  is workable and has not caused real -world
harm that would warrant its overruling
The status quo under  Williams  is eminently workable, and petitioner does not suggest otherwise.  After
Ballew, the rules of the road are clear:  juries in cases
involving serious criminal offenses must have at least
six jurors, but they need not have exactly 12.  Ballew,
435 U.S. at 239 (opinion of Blackmun, J.).  And petitioner cannot show that Williams  has led to any harmful “real-world consequences ,” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 122
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part) , that would justify
setting it aside.
In Ramos, it was self -evident that a rule permitting
nonunanimous juries led to guilty verdicts that would
have been hung juries in other States , thus leading to
the convictions “of some defendants who might not be
convicted under the proper constitutional rule.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 126 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in

24

part).  Petitioner argues  (Br. 35) that smaller juries
likewise will produce guilty verdicts more often, but
that is far from clear .  While larger juries might increase the chances of a holdout juror, they also might
make it easier for a dissenting voice to be drowned out.
Compare Pet. Br. 30 -34, with Resp. Br. 43 (collecting
competing  studies).  Such uncertainty  is not sufficient
to justify the disruption  of overruling Williams .
C. Petitioner’ s Arguments  Lack Merit
1. Petitioner errs in asserting  that this Court’s decision in Ramos already “effectively overruled Williams,” Pet. Br. 24 (capitalization  omitted), such that
stare decisis  should not even apply. Ramos held that
criminal juries must be unanimous, abrogating Apodaca v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972 )—not Williams .  See
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 93.  The mere fact that the plurality
opinion in the fractured Apadaca decision had relied on
Williams , see Pet. Br. 26 -27, does not mean that Apodaca and Williams must rise and fall together.   See
Burch, 441 U.S. at 13 9 (permitting six -person jury but
requiring unanimity) .  The Court in Ramos “d[id] not
claim that the Sixth Amendment incorporated every
feature of common -law practice,” 590 U.S. at 154 (Alito,
J., dissenting), and the jury’s size and unanimity are not
the same thing.
Nor are the principal flaws that Ramos identified in
the Apodaca plurality opinion  present  in Williams . A
key reason why several Justices in the Ramos majority
refused to retain Apodaca—Apodaca ’s unusual fracture, in which even the five Justices who agreed with
the result were opposed on the rationale, Ramos, 590
U.S. at 102 (opinion of Gorsuch, J.) —has no analogue in
the 7-1 decision in  Williams .  In addition,  the Apodaca
plurality “spent almost no time grappling” with history

25

or precedent and relied instead on “an incomplete functionalist analysis of its own creation for which it spared
one paragraph .”  Id. at 106  (majority opinion) .  Williams, however, explored  both history and precedent  at
length, and considered  the “function” of the historical
12-member practice only after its lengthy historical and
textual analysis.  399 U.S. at 99; see id. at 91-101.
2. Petitioner also fails to show that Williams was
“grievously or egregiously wrong ,” Ramos, 590 U.S. at
121 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part).   Much of petitioner’s historical evidence (Br. 5 -11, 18)  shows only
that Founding Era criminal juries had 12 people, not
that a 12-person requirement is  embedded in the original meaning of the Amendment’s text .  The mere fact of
common-law practice no more illuminates the constitutional question here than it does the constitutional question of whether the Sixth Amendment restricts juries to
property -owning men —a requirement that petitioner
presumably does not seek to enshrine .
Petitioner’s reliance (Br. 7) on dictionaries is similarly question -begging.  Both dictionaries he cites  actually defined “jury” more broadly to cover bodies of different sizes , and both mention the 12 -person petit jury
only when describing  contemporary jury -trial practice
in England .  See Jacob  Dictionary  (defining a “jury” as
“a certain number of men , sworn to inquire of and try
the matter of fact ”); 1 Samuel Johnson, Dictionary of
the English Language  1151 (4th ed. 1773)  (defining a
jury as “a company of men, as twenty -four or twelve,
sworn to deliver a truth upon   * * *  evidence”).   Moreover, if those definitions were controlling, a jury could
consist only of “men.”
Petitioner  asserts that in the  first decades after the
Amendment’s ratification, “state courts uniformly held

26

that the term ‘trial by jury’ in their own constitutions
required 12 jurors.”  Pet. Br. 9; see id. at 19-20.  But
none of his examples  from that early period supports
that assertion .  Two of the cited cases were interpreting
distinctive language in state constitutio ns that expressly froze in place prior jury -trial practices .  See,
e.g., Emerick v. Harris, 1 Binn. 416, 42 8 (Pa. 1808) (interpreting  a provision  requiring  that “trial by jury shall
be as heretofore ”) (emphasis added); Whitehurst  v. Davis, 3 N.C.  (2 Hayw.)  113, 113 (1800 ) (per curiam ) ( addressing a provision that  expressly adopted “the ancient mode  of trial  by jury ” (N.C. Decl. of Rights Art.
XIV (1776), reprinted in  5 Thorpe 2788) ) (emphasis
added).  Another discussed the 12 -juror requirement
only in dictum.  See Zylstra v. City of Charleston, 1 S.C.L.
(1 Bay) 382, 389 (1794 ).  And  Holmes v. Walton (N.J.
1780), mentioned in  a footnote (see Pet. Br. 7 n.2), has
no surviving written decision , making it impossible to
know whether the court was actually “interpreting ” the
phrase “trial by jury” in its state constitution or simply
relying on “extrinsic  norms.”  Wayne D. Moore, Written
and Unwritten Constitutional Law in the Early
Founding Period , 7 Const. Comm ent. 341, 354 (1990) .
Petitioner ’s reliance (Br. 9, 20 -21) on state-court decisions from later in the 19th century is similarly misplaced.  As a threshold matter, some of those decisions
interpreted provisions with language different from the
Sixth Amendment ’s.  See, e.g., Cancemi v. People, 18
N.Y. 128, 135  (1858) (interpreting provision that trial by
jury “shall remain inviolate  forever”).  And some state
courts reached conclusions contrary to petitioner’s position here .  See, e.g., Allen v. State, 51 Ga. 264 (1874)
(“The right to trial by jury is one thing, the number of
persons who shall compose the jury is another.”) .  As

27

discussed above,  see pp. 15-16, supra, the late 19th century was actually a time of growing state experimentation with juries of fewer than 12 members —not a time
of universal devotion to a historical form of unknown

Petitioner’s citation s of 19th-century treatises do not
show otherwise.  Petitioner cites  James Wilson’s comment that “the undoubting and the unanimous sentiment of the twelve jurors is of indispensable necessity.”
2 Wilson 985.   But read in context, Wilson was describing unanimity , not 12 jurors , as “indispensable. ”  Ibid.
On the actual subject of jury size , as petitioner acknowledges, Wilson remarked that he felt “no peculiar predilection for the number twelve.”   Br. 21 n.7 (citation omitted).  Petitioner suggests (ibid.) that Wilson was simply

He downplays the relevant reliance interests, asserting
(Pet. Br. 37) that “the vast majority of states” require a

terms of imprisonment.”  But if a 12-juror requirement

petitioner contends , then 12 jurors will be required in

28

all trials to which the Sixth Amendment right attaches,
which include not only felony trials but trials of misdemeanor offenses that carry potential sentences of more

Petitioner does not point to real -world harms that

4. Petitioner also suggests  (Br. 36) that Florida’s

Reconstruction timing .  And the Florida Senate in

29

49-50; Census Office, Dep’t  of the Interior, Statistics of
the Population of the United States at the Tenth Census
5 Tbl. I(d) (June 1, 1880).
In any event, w hatever the reason for Florida’s original enactment, it reenacted its six -person jury rule in
1968, and its current practice  coheres with the majority

II. AT A MINIMUM , THIS COURT SHOULD CONFIRM
THAT FEWER THAN 12 JURORS MAY RETURN  A VER-
DICT IN EMERGENCY CIRUMSTANCES
By rule, the default size of a federal criminal jury is
“12 persons .”  Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(1) .  But under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 23(b)(3), “the court
may permit a jury of 11 persons to return a verdict, even
without stipulation by the parties, if the court finds good
cause to excuse a juror”  after “ the jury has retired to
deliberate .”  As petitioner recognize s, Rule 23(b)(3) is
meaningfully different from laws like Florida’s, which
address the default size of a jury, because Rule 23(b)(3)
involves the procedures applied “  ‘when an emergency
arises toward the end of the deliberations’ rather than
the number of jurors who must be sworn at the outset.”
Pet. Br. 13 n.4 (citation omitted).   Regardless of whether
the Sixth Amendment requires empaneling a jury of 12
at the outset of trial, there is no basis to conclude that
the Amendment  bars Rule 23(b)(3)’s emergency procedures.  Accordingly, even if this Court holds that petitioner’s Sixth Amendment rights were violated , it
should not adopt a rule that calls the constitutionality of
Rule 23(b)(3)  into question .

30

A. As jury-trial practice has evolved, so have the procedures to remedy  a juror’s unexpected  dismissal .  At
common law , if a juror “disappeared or became incapacitated” during trial , the ordinary common -law remedy
was a new trial.  Hinton v. United States , 979 A.2d 663,
672 (D.C. 2009)  (en banc) .  The 11 remaining jurors
would be retained, and the judge would select a twelfth.
With the jury reconstituted , the trial began anew.   Ibid.
With only minor differences, the same practice prevailed in early American trials.  Ibid.; see  Nancy J.
King, Juror Delinquency in Criminal Trials in America, 1796 -1996, 94 Mich. L. Rev. 2673, 2726 (1996).
Such retrials would not have been  particularly burdensome, given the “astonishing rapidity of trial and
verdict,” Langbein 27 , at the time.  Eighteenth -century
criminal trials typically lasted less than one hour from
start to finish.  See Sir John Baker, An Introduction to
English Legal History  551 & n.66 ( 5th ed. 2019); King
2681.  Jury deliberations, in turn, often lasted only a few
minutes.  See Langbein 27 ; King 2710 .  If the jury retired to a separate room to deliberate, they would be
locked together (including overnight ) without food , at
least in part  to encourage a quick decision .  King 2678 -
2679; see  3 Blackstone 375 .
As American criminal trials became significantly
longer and more complex, mistrials due to juror incapacitation became more frequent and retrials more
costly.  See King 2709-2712; Hinton, 979 A.2d at 675;
H.R. Rep. No. 957, 72d Cong., 1st Sess. , at 1 (1932)
(House Report).   New practices developed  in the late
19th and early 20th centuries  to address those novel
burdens .  For example, this Court held that parties
could stipulate to a verdict by a smaller jury when a juror dropped out.  See Patton, 281 U.S. at 306-307.  States

31

and Congress  also provide d for alternate jurors who
would hear the evidence alongside the selected jurors
and could replace one who became incapacitated .  See
Act of June 29, 1932, ch.  309, 47 Stat. 380 -381; House
Report 2 .  Although the concept of alternate jurors
would have been unfamiliar to the Framers,  see King
2726, today they are nearly universal .
B. The current federal rules accordingly allow
courts, when a juror is dismissed after deliberations
have already begun , to replace the dismissed juror with
an alternate and “instruct the jury to begin its deliberations anew.”  Fed. R. Crim. P. 24(c)(3).   But depending
on the circumstances , it may “not [be] desirab le to allow
a juror who is unfamiliar with the prior del iberations to
suddenly join the group and participate in the voting
without the benefit of earlier group discussion.”  3 The
ABA Standards for Criminal Justice  § 15 -2.7, comm.
(2d ed. 1980) .  And inserting  an alternate and restarting
deliberations can add delays that could cause even  more
jurors to become unavailable .  See , e.g., United States
v. Levenite , 277 F.3d 454 , 465  (4th Cir.) , cert. denied,
535 U.S. 1005 (2002) .
Rule 23(b)(3)  avoids those concerns  by permitting
the court , in its discretion,  to allow the remaining 11 jurors to deliver a verdict in the event that a juror is dismissed for good cause after the start of deliberations .
See Fed. R. Crim. P. 23(b)(3) advisory committee’s note
(1983 Amendment ).  Since its adoption in 1983, Rule
23(b)(3) has spared many cases from burdensome restarts when a juror is  unexpectedly excused  for good
cause during deliberations.  See, e.g., Levenite , 277 F.3d
464 (juror became ill  with contagious intestinal flu  during deliberations ); United States  v. Chorney, 63 F.3d 78,

32

81 (1st Cir. 1995)  (juror’s son was killed during deliberations); United States  v. Wilson, 894 F.2d 1245, 1250
(11th Cir.) (pregnant juror became ill and feared a miscarriage) , cert. denied, 497 U.S. 1029 (1990) .
C. The Sixth Amendment does not prohibit  Rule
23(b)(3)’s remedy for the mid -deliberation  dismissal  of
a juror.  Even if the common law would have required a
retrial before 12 jurors , there is no reason to believe
that practice  was so definitional to the meaning of a trial
by jury  as to be embedded in the Sixth Amendment .
The Fou nding Era remedies for  juror dismissal were
“justified by conditions which no longer exist ,” Patton,
281 U.S. at 306, and which were starkly different from
conditions today.
This Court has already dispensed with common -law
deliberation practices  that are impractical for modern
trials, like the requirement that that jury continuously
be sequestered, without even a “lunch break [ ],” until it
reached a verdict.  Dietz, 579 U.S. at 5 2.  The practice
of ending deliberations —and redoing the entire trial —
on the loss of even one juror is of a piece.  Mandatory
retrials  were relatively easy when trials  typically  lasted
less than an hour , but they are not a satisfactory  solution in a world with  longer and more complex trials .  If
they were immutably enshrined in the Sixth Amendment, then even the ubiquitous modern remedy of substituting in an alternate  juror would be impermissible .
The trial, no matter how long and complex, would need
to begin anew, with the attendant burdens on the witnesses, the court, the government, and the defendant
himself.  Nothing justifies that result.

33

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, t he judgment of the Florida Fourth District Court of Appeal  should be affirmed .
